Day 40 of 100 · Infrastructure Automation

LAMP Automation Capstone

#100DaysOfCloudAndSecurityInfrastructure AutomationPublished journey entry

The Ansible phase closed by combining roles for common setup, Apache, PHP and MySQL into a deployable LAMP stack with Vault, handlers and failure recovery.

Architecture / mental model

control node → site.yml → common/apache/php/mysql roles → target host → HTTP + database services

How it works

The capstone moved beyond isolated syntax and connected reusable roles into one deployment. Common host setup, web server configuration, PHP and database responsibilities were separated so each role remained understandable.

Sensitive values were kept out of plain playbook logic with Vault. Handlers connected configuration changes to service actions instead of restarting services unconditionally.

The lab also exposed real operational failures: package-manager return behavior around MySQL and a port-80 conflict later in the deployment. Those failures are more valuable evidence than a perfect demo because they force the automation to encode what recovery and verification actually mean.

Hands-on reference

ansible-playbook -i hosts.ini site.yml --ask-vault-pass
ansible all -i hosts.ini -m ping

Verification

Verify Ansible reachability first, run the play, then test the HTTP endpoint, expected services and database state from the target. Re-run to confirm convergence after the environment is corrected.

Field note / gotcha

The capstone hit package/return-code and port-conflict realities. Automation must distinguish an expected package-manager condition from an actual failed desired state, and a service cannot bind a port another process already owns.

Security considerations

Keep database secrets encrypted, minimize sudo scope, firewall the host and expose only the services the architecture requires.

What I learned

A capstone earns its value when multiple layers fail together and the operator can still explain exactly which layer broke.

Evidence note: Published phase capstone evidence and project failure history. The blog expands the technical explanation; it does not claim every paragraph is verbatim from the original social post.
